```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(mzLibR)
# Every call on this page is answered from a recording of the real bridge, made on the reference
# tables this package ships in extdata/stats/, so the page builds anywhere. With a bridge
# installed, the same calls compute the answers.
.mzlibr_example <- mzLibR:::replay_bridge_start()
```

Most proteomics differential-abundance analyses end in limma: a linear model per protein, with
each protein's noisy variance shrunk toward what all the proteins together say (empirical-Bayes
moderation, Smyth 2004). R has limma. These functions are the same method **computed by mzLib**,
so an analysis in R reports the statistics MetaMorpheus and the Python and Rust bindings report,
from the same code. The first section lets you check the agreement rather than take it on trust.

| question | function | mzLib | method |
|---|---|---|---|
| which features change with a coefficient, and how surely? | `stats_fit()` | `LinearModel.Fit`, `EmpiricalBayes.Moderate` (#1341) | limma `lmFit` + `eBayes(legacy = TRUE)` |
| which of my p-values survive a false discovery rate? | `stats_adjust()` | `MultipleTesting.BenjaminiHochberg` | Benjamini and Hochberg 1995 |
| what is one feature's effect, pooled across studies? | `stats_meta()` | `RandomEffectsMeta.Pool` (#1357) | DerSimonian and Laird 1986, as metafor `rma(method = "DL")` |
| which features differ by a contrast, within what interval? | `stats_fit(contrasts = )` | `EmpiricalBayes.ModerateContrasts` (#1452) | limma `contrasts.fit` + `topTable(confint = )` |
| what do several studies' p-values say together? | `stats_combine_p()` | `PValueCombination.Fisher`, `.Stouffer` (#1367) | Fisher 1925, Stouffer 1949 |
| which features rise or fall with a per-sample trait? | `stats_correlate()` | `SpearmanCorrelation.Correlate`, `.PartialCorrelate` (#1367, #1446) | R `cor.test(method = "spearman")`, ppcor `pcor.test` |
| does a 0/1 outcome (detected or not) follow a coefficient? | `stats_fit_logistic()` | `LogisticRegression.Fit` (#1367) | R `glm(family = binomial)` per feature |
| which features change, when samples come in groups? | `stats_fit_mixed()` | `MixedModel.Fit` (#1367) | `nlme::lme()` with a random intercept per group |
| does a search really control its FDR? | `stats_entrapment_fdp()` | `EntrapmentFdp.Sweep` (#1385) | Wen et al. 2025, as FDRBench |

`stats_fit()` already adjusts its own p-values, so you need `stats_adjust()` only for p-values
from somewhere else, and `stats_meta()` only when you have one estimate per study.

## Check it against limma

mzLib's test suite carries a frozen limma run: 400 features, 12 samples with missing values, a
design of intercept, age in decades and sex, and limma's `eBayes` output for the age coefficient.
This package ships the input and limma's output in `extdata/stats/`:

```{r}
data <- system.file("extdata", "stats", package = "mzLibR")
fit <- stats_fit(file.path(data, "limma_reference_responses.tsv"),
                 file.path(data, "limma_reference_design.tsv"), "age_decades")
fit
fit$coefficient_names
```

Compare every feature with what limma said:

```{r}
limma <- read.delim(file.path(data, "limma_ebayes_notrend.tsv"))
worst <- function(ours, theirs) max(abs(ours - theirs) / abs(theirs))
c(t = worst(fit$records$t, limma$t_age),
  p_value = worst(fit$records$p_value, limma$p_age),
  bh_adjusted = worst(fit$records$bh_adjusted, limma$bh_age),
  posterior_variance = worst(fit$records$posterior_variance, limma$s2_post),
  df_total = worst(fit$records$df_total, limma$df_total))
```

Every relative difference is below 1e-8. With limma installed you can run it yourself on the same
input, `limma::eBayes(limma::lmFit(y, x), legacy = TRUE)`; this package's tests do exactly that,
and `bh_adjusted` is `p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH")`.

**Which limma: the *legacy* estimator.** This matches `eBayes(legacy = TRUE)`. When features have
different residual degrees of freedom, limma 3.61 and later default to a different prior
estimator. Omitting missing values per feature is exactly what makes residual df differ, so on
most label-free data default limma reports a slightly different prior and different moderated
statistics. The fit says when your input is such a case:

```{r}
fit$residual_df_differ
```

## A real experiment with a known answer

mzLib's RNA test data (mzLib #1388) holds a dilution series - real mass-spectrometry data where the
right answer is known in advance. Across 27 runs the lncRNA **MALAT1** was loaded at 500, 250 or
125 ng, while the luciferase transcript **FLuc** stayed at 500 ng. Halving MALAT1 should read as a
log2 fold change of -1, quartering it as -2.

The responses are each oligo's log2 FlashLFQ intensity minus that run's median log2 intensity of
the FLuc-only oligos (blank where FlashLFQ detected nothing), one row per oligo named
`<transcript>:<sequence>`. The design has an intercept, so each coefficient is the change from the
500 ng runs:

```{r}
design <- read.delim(file.path(data, "malat_dilution_design.tsv"))
table(malat_250ng = design$malat_250ng, malat_125ng = design$malat_125ng)
fit <- stats_fit(file.path(data, "malat_dilution_log2_vs_fluc.tsv"),
                 file.path(data, "malat_dilution_design.tsv"), c("malat_250ng", "malat_125ng"))
fit$status_counts
```

**Most oligos could not be fitted, and the fit says why rather than dropping them.** An oligo seen
in two or three runs has no residual variance to estimate (`too_few_observations`); one seen only
in the 500 ng runs cannot have a 250 ng effect (`rank_deficient`). Both are rows with `NA`
statistics, and neither enters the Benjamini-Hochberg family.

The question the experiment was designed to answer, as the median log2 fold change per
transcript:

```{r}
fitted <- fit$records[fit$records$status == "fitted", ]
fitted$transcript <- sub(":.*$", "", fitted$feature)
keep <- fitted$transcript %in% c("MALAT1", "FLuc")
aggregate(estimate ~ transcript + coefficient, data = fitted[keep, ], FUN = median)
```

**Half the MALAT1 reads as about -0.9 against a known -1; a quarter reads as about -1 against a
known -2.** The second is compressed by about half. The statistics did not create that: the
estimates are ordinary least squares, and moderation changes only their standard errors. FLuc
sits near 0 largely by construction, since every run was normalised to it.

Which oligos pass a 5% false discovery rate?

```{r}
hits <- fitted[!is.na(fitted$bh_adjusted) & fitted$bh_adjusted < 0.05, ]
table(hits$coefficient, hits$transcript)
```

**Few, and not all of them true.** Two of the quarter-load calls are 20-mer oligos, loaded at a
constant amount. A 5% false discovery rate bounds the expected share of wrong calls; it does not
promise none, and a known-answer experiment is how you see it happen.

### Unequal degrees of freedom: the marginal-likelihood prior

This experiment is the case the note on limma's legacy estimator warns about: oligos are missing
from different runs, so they have different residual degrees of freedom, and the default prior is
limma's legacy estimator:

```{r}
c(residual_df_differ = fit$residual_df_differ, estimator = fit$prior$estimator,
  prior_df = round(fit$prior$df, 1))
```

mzLib has a second estimator for exactly this case, `"marginal_likelihood"` (mzLib #1368). It fits
the prior by maximum likelihood with **each oligo's own degrees of freedom**, so an oligo seen in
five runs counts as five runs' worth of evidence about the variance, not as an average one. Ask
for it by name:

```{r}
ml <- stats_fit(file.path(data, "malat_dilution_log2_vs_fluc.tsv"),
                file.path(data, "malat_dilution_design.tsv"), c("malat_250ng", "malat_125ng"),
                estimator = "marginal_likelihood")
c(estimator = ml$prior$estimator, prior_df = round(ml$prior$df, 1))
ml_fitted <- ml$records[ml$records$status == "fitted", ]
ml_hits <- ml_fitted[!is.na(ml_fitted$bh_adjusted) & ml_fitted$bh_adjusted < 0.05, ]
table(ml_hits$coefficient, sub(":.*$", "", ml_hits$feature))
```

**The prior df falls**: once each oligo's own degrees of freedom count, the data support less
shrinkage toward the common variance. The estimates are the same least-squares numbers; only the
standard errors move, and with them the calls - compare this table with the one above. At half load
the FLuc call is gone, which is right, since FLuc did not change.

- **It is mzLib's own estimator, not limma's.** Default limma (3.61 and later) handles unequal
  degrees of freedom with a different method (`fitFDistUnequalDF1`), so expect small differences
  from default limma.
- **mzLib keeps `"moments_legacy"` the default**, so that `stats_fit()` reproduces
  `eBayes(legacy = TRUE)` exactly. Leaving `estimator` out always means mzLib's default, and
  `prior$estimator` says which one you got.
- **A prior df of about 0.05 is a floor, not a finding.** mzLib searches d0 from e^-3 upward.
- One prior serves the whole call: every coefficient and every contrast is moderated with it.

## Contrasts: any comparison, with a confidence interval

A design's coefficients answer one kind of question: each level against the baseline. The
questions a scientist asks are often other comparisons: 500 ng against 250 ng when the baseline is
125 ng, or the mean of two groups against a third. Each is a **contrast**, a weighted sum of the
coefficients, and `stats_fit(contrasts = )` tests it with the same moderated t, plus a confidence
interval: limma's `contrasts.fit()`, `eBayes()` and `topTable(confint = 0.95)`.

You rarely write the weights yourself. `diff_design()` builds the design from your sample sheet
and writes the contrasts beside it. With no reference level, every pair of levels is a contrast:

```{r}
samples <- system.file("extdata", "diff", "malat_dilution_samples.tsv", package = "mzLibR")
design <- diff_design(samples, factors = list(factor_spec("malat_load")),
                      out = file.path(tempdir(), "malat_pairs"))
stratum <- design$strata[[1]]
stratum$column_names
stratum$warnings
labels <- setNames(design$records$label, design$records$contrast_id)
labels
```

mzLib took the first level, 125 ng, as the coding baseline, and wrote `design_1.tsv` and
`contrasts_1.tsv`. Fit the design and test every contrast in the file. No coefficient is named, so
the coefficient table is empty and every answer is in `contrasts`:

```{r}
pairs <- stats_fit(file.path(data, "malat_dilution_log2_vs_fluc.tsv"), stratum$design_file,
                   contrasts = stratum$contrasts_file)
pairs$contrasts
c(coefficient_rows = pairs$row_count, contrast_rows = pairs$contrasts$row_count)
```

The weights are on `pairs$coefficient_names`. `c1` and `c2` are single coefficients. **`c3` is
not**: it is the 500 ng coefficient minus the 250 ng one, a comparison no column of this design
holds. The answers are known in advance, +1, +2 and +1 in log2, so look at the MALAT1 oligos:

```{r}
known <- c(c1 = 1, c2 = 2, c3 = 1)
summary_of <- function(id) {
  r <- pairs$contrasts$records
  r <- r[r$contrast == id & r$status == "fitted" & startsWith(r$feature, "MALAT1:"), ]
  c(known = known[[id]], median = round(median(r$estimate), 2), oligos = nrow(r),
    interval_holds_it = sum(r$confidence_low <= known[[id]] & known[[id]] <= r$confidence_high),
    excludes_zero = sum(!(r$confidence_low <= 0 & 0 <= r$confidence_high)))
}
t(sapply(c("c1", "c2", "c3"), summary_of))
```

- **Each oligo's 95% interval is wide.** It holds the known change for most oligos, and also holds
  0 for most of them: one oligo, measured in a handful of runs, cannot tell a doubling from no
  change. The medians across oligos are much more precise than any one interval.
- **The contrasts locate the compression seen above.** 500 ng against 250 ng reads close to its
  known +1; 250 ng against 125 ng reads far less. The shortfall is between the two lower loads.
- **The intervals are per feature and not adjusted.** For a decision across features use
  `bh_adjusted`, which each contrast has over its own fitted features.

Each row of `pairs$contrasts$records` carries what a coefficient row does, plus `confidence_low`
and `confidence_high`, in response units per contrast unit: a log2 fold change here.

**Your own contrasts.** A contrasts file is a header of a contrast id column and then exactly the
design's coefficient columns, in any order, then one row per contrast: its id and one weight per
coefficient. To compare the mean of 250 ng and 125 ng against 500 ng on the design above:

```text
contrast           intercept  malat_load=250ng  malat_load=500ng
low_mean_vs_500    0          0.5               -1
```

(125 ng is the baseline, so its coefficient is 0 and needs no weight of its own.) A column the
design lacks, a design column the file lacks, a weight that is not a number, or a row of all zeros
is refused.

The traps:

- **Contrast ids are numbered within each stratum**, so `c1` can mean different comparisons in two
  strata. Read the labels from `diff_design()`, as above.
- **With missing values the standard error is exact per feature**, computed on the samples that
  feature was observed in. limma's `contrasts.fit()` approximates it there, so on data with missing
  values these numbers differ from limma's by design; with complete data they agree.
- **A contrast of one coefficient is that coefficient's test**, number for number. Asking for both
  in one call costs nothing: the model is fitted once and the prior is shared.
- `confidence = 0.9` (a fraction) changes the level; leave it out for mzLib's default, and
  `contrasts$confidence_level` reports the level used.
- **It needs the pyMzLib 0.6.0 bridge.** An older bridge ignores `--contrasts` and `--estimator`, so
  `stats_fit()` stops with an error naming the bridge it needs rather than return a fit that did
  not do what you asked.

## Your own data

`stats_fit()` reads two tab-separated files: a **responses** table, one row per feature and one
column per sample, and a **design**, one row per sample, matched to the responses' columns by
name. `write.table(x, path, sep = "\t", quote = FALSE)` writes either. Three things decide
whether the answer means what you think:

- **Log-transform first.** The model is additive in whatever you pass; with log2 intensities,
  `estimate` is a log2 fold change.
- **A 0 is an observation.** Many quantification tables write 0 for "not measured". Make those
  cells `NA`, or they are fitted as a real zero; `zero_count` counts them and a caveat says so.
- **The design is used as written.** Include the intercept column yourself. `diff_design()` writes
  one from a sample sheet, with a contrasts file for any comparison that is no single column; see
  `vignette("diff", package = "mzLibR")`.

## P-values from anywhere

```{r}
adjusted <- stats_adjust(c(0.0002, 0.004, 0.019, NA, 0.031, 0.2, NaN, 0.74))
adjusted$tested_count
adjusted$records
```

`NA` marks a feature that was not tested: it stays `NA` and is not counted in m. Do not write 1
for it; that enlarges the family.

## Pooling across studies

`stats_meta()` takes one row per study - `feature`, `estimate`, `standard_error` - and pools each
feature with the DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model. These are metafor's own reference cases,
from mzLib's test data:

```{r}
inputs <- read.delim(file.path(data, "metafor_dl_inputs.tsv"))
pooled <- stats_meta(data.frame(feature = inputs$case, estimate = inputs$yi,
                                standard_error = inputs$sei))
pooled$records[, c("feature", "studies", "estimate", "tau2", "i_squared", "direction_agree",
                   "direction_disagree", "leave_one_out_max_delta")]
metafor <- read.delim(file.path(data, "metafor_dl_results.tsv"))
worst(pooled$records$estimate[match(metafor$case, pooled$records$feature)], metafor$estimate)
```

`direction_agree` and `leave_one_out_max_delta` are the two checks a reader of a pooled result
asks for first: how many studies point the same way, and how far the answer moves without any one
of them. The interval uses a normal reference and does not widen for few studies, so treat a
pooled estimate from two or three studies with care.

## Combining p-values across studies

Sometimes all you have from each study is a p-value. `stats_combine_p()` turns several independent
p-values for the same feature into one, by one of two rules: `"fisher"`, X = -2 sum ln p against
chi-square on 2k degrees of freedom, driven by the smallest p-values; or `"stouffer"`,
Z = sum w z / sqrt(sum w^2) against the standard normal, which weighs every study (for example by
the square root of its sample size). There is no default: mzLib prefers neither, so you choose.
mzLib's own reference cases show the difference:

```{r}
cases <- read.delim(file.path(data, "combination_inputs.tsv"))
cases[cases$case == "mixed", ]
fisher <- stats_combine_p(data.frame(feature = cases$case, p_value = cases$p), method = "fisher")
stouffer <- stats_combine_p(data.frame(feature = cases$case, p_value = cases$p, weight = cases$weight),
                            method = "stouffer")
data.frame(feature = fisher$records$feature, studies = fisher$records$studies,
           fisher = signif(fisher$records$p_value, 3), weighted_stouffer = signif(stouffer$records$p_value, 3))
```

In `mixed`, one p-value of 0.001 sits among four that disagree. Fisher says the five studies
together are significant, because one of them is; weighted Stouffer says they are not, because the
heaviest study points the other way. Both agree with R's `pchisq()` and `qnorm()`:

```{r}
r_answers <- read.delim(file.path(data, "combination_results.tsv"))
c(fisher = worst(fisher$records$p_value, r_answers$fisher_p),
  weighted_stouffer = worst(stouffer$records$p_value, r_answers$weighted_p))
```

**The trap: two-sided p-values have no direction.** Both rules combine *one-sided* p-values. A
two-sided p-value - which is what `stats_fit()` reports - says how surprising an effect is, not
which way it went, so two studies that disagree count as two that agree. Here are three proteins,
each tested in three cohorts (illustrative numbers, written here, not measured):

```{r}
cohorts <- data.frame(
  feature = rep(c("up_everywhere", "flips_sign", "no_effect"), each = 3),
  p_value = c(0.003, 0.02, 0.3, 0.001, 0.004, 0.4, 0.6, 0.45, 0.85),
  weight = c(4, 5, 3, 4, 5, 3, 4, 5, 3),
  effect = c(0.8, 0.5, 0.3, 1.2, -0.9, 0.2, -0.1, 0.1, -0.05))
ignored <- stats_combine_p(cohorts[, c("feature", "p_value", "weight")], method = "stouffer")
signed <- stats_combine_p(cohorts, method = "stouffer")
data.frame(feature = signed$records$feature, direction_ignored = signif(ignored$records$p_value, 2),
           signed = signif(signed$records$p_value, 2))
```

**Ignoring direction, `flips_sign` is the strongest result of the three**: it rose sharply in one
cohort and fell sharply in another. Give each test its `effect` (only its sign is used) and mzLib
first turns each two-sided p into the one-sided p-value for effect > 0, so opposite effects cancel.
The combined `p_value` is the **upper tail**: signed, it tests effect > 0, and a Stouffer `p_value`
near 1 means a consistently negative effect.

Before you trust a combined p-value: the studies must be independent (two analyses of the same
samples are one study); it is not adjusted across features (send `records$p_value` to
`stats_adjust()`); and it is not an effect size. If every study reports an estimate and a standard
error on one scale, `stats_meta()` pools those and says how much the studies disagree; prefer it.

## Correlating features with a trait

When the samples differ by a number rather than a group - age, dose, the amount loaded - the
question is which features rise or fall with it. `stats_correlate()` answers it with Spearman's
rank correlation: for each feature, mzLib ranks the feature's values and the trait over the
samples where both are known, correlates the ranks, and tests rho = 0, two-sided. It reads
`stats_fit()`'s responses table and a **trait** table: one row per sample, then one value column,
whose header names the trait.

```{r}
correlation <- stats_correlate(file.path(data, "malat_dilution_log2_vs_fluc.tsv"),
                               file.path(data, "malat_dilution_load_ng.tsv"))
correlation
r <- correlation$records
r$transcript <- sub(":.*$", "", r$feature)
estimable <- r[r$method != "not_estimable" & r$transcript %in% c("MALAT1", "FLuc", "20mer2"), ]
aggregate(rho ~ transcript, data = estimable, FUN = median)
```

MALAT1's oligos rise with its load, and FLuc's, the spike every run was normalised to, do not.

- `method` says how `p_value` was computed: `"exact"` (the full permutation distribution, for n of
  9 or fewer with no ties, as R's `cor.test()`), `"asymptotic"` (t on n - 2 degrees of freedom, as
  `cor.test(exact = FALSE)`), or `"not_estimable"`, where `rho` and `p_value` are `NA`.
- **Small n cannot be significant.** Three samples have six orderings, so even a perfect rank
  correlation on three runs has p = 1/3.
- **An asymptotic p-value of exactly 0 means rho is exactly -1 or 1**: the t-test's limit, not a
  measured probability.
- **For 10 to 1289 samples without ties, R's default `cor.test()` uses an Edgeworth series** that
  mzLib does not, so p-values there differ slightly from R's default output, but not from
  `cor.test(exact = FALSE)`. This package's tests hold every row to `cor.test()` run in R.

**Partial correlation.** If something else also varies by sample - batch, run order, sex - give it
in a `given` table of the same shape. mzLib then correlates what is left of the feature's ranks and
the trait's ranks after each is regressed on the covariates' ranks, as
`ppcor::pcor.test(method = "spearman")` does:

```{r}
plain <- stats_correlate(file.path(data, "limma_reference_responses.tsv"),
                         file.path(data, "limma_reference_age.tsv"))
partial <- stats_correlate(file.path(data, "limma_reference_responses.tsv"),
                           file.path(data, "limma_reference_age.tsv"),
                           given = file.path(data, "limma_reference_sex.tsv"))
rbind(plain = plain$method_counts, given_sex = partial$method_counts)
head(data.frame(feature = plain$records$feature, rho = round(plain$records$rho, 2),
                rho_given_sex = round(partial$records$rho, 2)), 5)
```

The partial test is always asymptotic, on n - 2 - k degrees of freedom for k covariates. Partial
out only nuisance variables: a covariate that follows the trait takes the trait's signal with it.

## Is a feature's detection related to the condition?

Missing values in label-free data are rarely random: a protein near the detection limit is missed
more often where there is less of it. Ask the data first: **does each feature's chance of being
detected depend on the condition?** That is a logistic regression per feature on a table of 1
(measured) and 0 (not measured). `stats_fit_logistic()` runs one per feature, as R's
`glm(family = binomial)`, and tests each coefficient with a Wald z. The dilution series has a
detection table: 1 where the responses file has a value, 0 where it is blank.

```{r}
detection <- stats_fit_logistic(file.path(data, "malat_dilution_detected.tsv"),
                                file.path(data, "malat_dilution_design.tsv"),
                                c("malat_250ng", "malat_125ng"))
detection$status_counts
quarter <- detection$records[detection$records$coefficient == "malat_125ng", ]
quarter$transcript <- sub(":.*$", "", quarter$feature)
detected <- quarter[quarter$status == "fitted" & quarter$transcript %in% c("MALAT1", "FLuc"), ]
aggregate(estimate ~ transcript, data = detected, FUN = median)
```

`estimate` is a change in the **log-odds** of detection: for a 0/1 column, the log of the odds
ratio against the 500 ng runs.

**A separated feature has no estimate, and that is not the same as no effect.** When the design
splits a feature's 0s from its 1s, no maximum-likelihood estimate exists. R's `glm()` prints a
huge coefficient and a warning there; mzLib reports `"separated"` and `NA`. Most oligos here are
separated because they were seen in a handful of runs, or none:

```{r}
separated <- quarter[quarter$status == "separated", ]
head(sort(table(events = separated$events), decreasing = TRUE), 4)
```

Here separation means "too sparse to say". In a cleaner experiment the same status can mark the
strongest result in the table - a protein detected in every treated sample and in no control - so
read `events` and `observed` before you discard one. Against R's `glm()`, on mzLib's own reference
input:

```{r}
glm_fit <- stats_fit_logistic(file.path(data, "glm_reference_responses.tsv"),
                              file.path(data, "glm_reference_design.tsv"), c("Intercept", "x", "grp"))
glm <- read.delim(file.path(data, "glm_reference_fit.tsv"))
x <- glm_fit$records[glm_fit$records$coefficient == "x", ]
ok <- glm$status == "fitted"
c(estimate = worst(x$estimate[ok], glm$b1[ok]), standard_error = worst(x$standard_error[ok], glm$se1[ok]))
```

The estimates agree to better than 1e-8 and the standard errors to 1e-6 (`summary.glm()` takes its
weights from the step before the estimate). Wald tests are weakest near separation and in small
samples, and no likelihood-ratio test is offered. A 0 is an outcome: blank only a cell you
genuinely do not know.

## When samples come in groups

Runs acquired on different days, replicates from one donor, studies pooled into one analysis: each
group can sit at its own baseline. `stats_fit()` treats every sample as independent, so a
day-to-day shift either inflates its residual variance or, when the days are unbalanced, leaks into
the effect. A **mixed model** gives every group its own baseline, a random intercept with variance
tau^2, and estimates each coefficient *within* groups: `stats_fit_mixed()`, as
`nlme::lme(y ~ ..., random = ~ 1 | group)` per feature. The dilution series' runs were acquired on
five days; a **groups** table says which:

```{r}
mixed <- stats_fit_mixed(file.path(data, "malat_dilution_log2_vs_fluc.tsv"),
                         file.path(data, "malat_dilution_design.tsv"),
                         file.path(data, "malat_dilution_day.tsv"), c("malat_250ng", "malat_125ng"))
mixed
malat_medians <- function(result) {
  r <- result$records[result$records$status == "fitted" & startsWith(result$records$feature, "MALAT1:"), ]
  aggregate(cbind(estimate, standard_error) ~ coefficient, data = r, FUN = median)
}
malat_medians(fit)
malat_medians(mixed)
```

The design is unchanged: do not add a column per day, the random intercept replaces it.
`estimator` is `"reml"` because none was given and that is mzLib's default. Within days, the median
standard errors are smaller: the day-to-day shift no longer counts as noise.

- **A coefficient constant within each group is tested on the groups.** Its `df` is nlme's
  "containment" df, a whole number per row; with too few groups there is none, and `p_value` is `NA`
  while `t` is reported.
- **`group_variance` 0 is the boundary**: no group effect. nlme cannot reach 0 and reports a tiny
  positive value there instead.
- **Under `"reml"` the log-likelihood is restricted**: compare it only between models with the same
  fixed effects, and use `estimator = "ml"` to compare designs.

Against nlme, on mzLib's own reference input (seven groups of unequal size):

```{r}
lmm <- stats_fit_mixed(file.path(data, "lmm_reference_responses.tsv"),
                       file.path(data, "lmm_reference_design.tsv"),
                       file.path(data, "lmm_reference_groups.tsv"), c("Intercept", "age", "wp"))
nlme <- read.delim(file.path(data, "lmm_reference_fit.tsv"))
nlme <- nlme[nlme$method == "REML", ]
age <- lmm$records[lmm$records$coefficient == "age", ]
c(estimate = worst(age$estimate, nlme$b1), standard_error = worst(age$standard_error, nlme$se1))
all(age$df == nlme$df1)
```

mzLib matches nlme to 1e-5 relative (nlme's own optimizer precision). Satterthwaite and
Kenward-Roger df (lmerTest) are not implemented, so p-values differ from lmerTest's.

## Does a search really control its FDR?

An entrapment experiment adds peptides that cannot be in the sample to the search database. Every
entrapment the search reports is then a known false discovery, which lets you check the search's
FDR claim instead of trusting it. `stats_entrapment_fdp()` computes the three valid estimators of
Wen et al. 2025 at each q-value threshold: `lower_bound` (above your claimed FDR, the search fails
to control it; below, it proves nothing), `combined` (an upper bound: at or below your claimed FDR,
evidence of control) and `paired` (a tighter upper bound for 1:1 pairing). The "sample" estimator
N_E / (r N_T) is invalid in both directions and is deliberately absent.

```{r}
fdp <- stats_entrapment_fdp(file.path(data, "entrapment_reference_targets.tsv"),
                            file.path(data, "entrapment_reference_entrapments.tsv"), ratio = 1)
fdp
fdp$records[fdp$records$q_value_threshold %in% c(0.003, 0.01), ]
```

This is mzLib's hand-built search: seven targets and four entrapments. At 1% the search reports 7
discoveries, 3 of them entrapments: far from a 1% FDR. Give one row per unit you estimate for
(precursor, peptide or protein group), decoys removed, each with its best q-value; mzLib does not
deduplicate. `ratio` is required: mzLib has no default, and `paired` is reported only at a ratio of
exactly 1, so for 1:1 pairing pass 1, not a ratio computed from database sizes after exclusions.

The methods and resources behind the functions on this page, from their specs:

- [doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1995.tb02031.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1995.tb02031.x): the step-up adjustment (Benjamini and Hochberg, J R Stat Soc B 57:289, 1995).
- [doi:10.1111/j.1420-9101.2005.00917.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1420-9101.2005.00917.x): the weighted Z (Stouffer) method and why it outperforms Fisher's for a shared effect (Whitlock, J Evol Biol 18:1368, 2005).
- [doi:10.2307/1412159](https://doi.org/10.2307/1412159): the rank correlation coefficient rho (Spearman, Am J Psychol 15:72, 1904).
- [doi:10.5351/CSAM.2015.22.6.665](https://doi.org/10.5351/CSAM.2015.22.6.665): ppcor, whose pcor.test(method = 'spearman') the partial form (--given) reproduces (Kim, Commun Stat Appl Methods 22:665, 2015).
- [doi:10.2307/2347111](https://doi.org/10.2307/2347111): the Edgeworth series (AS 89) R's cor.test uses by default for 10 <= n < 1290, which mzLib does NOT use (Best and Roberts, Appl Stat 24:377, 1975).
- [doi:10.1038/s41592-025-02719-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-025-02719-x): the lower-bound (eq. 2), combined (eq. 1) and paired (eq. 4) entrapment estimators mzLib implements, and why the sample estimator is invalid (Wen et al., Nat Methods 22:1454, 2025; the method FDRBench implements).
- [doi:10.2307/2344614](https://doi.org/10.2307/2344614): generalized linear models and their fitting by iteratively reweighted least squares, the estimator mzLib implements (Nelder and Wedderburn, J R Stat Soc A 135:370, 1972).
- [doi:10.1093/biomet/71.1.1](https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/71.1.1): separation: when the outcomes are split by the design the maximum-likelihood estimate does not exist, which is the separated status (Albert and Anderson, Biometrika 71:1, 1984).
- [doi:10.2307/2529876](https://doi.org/10.2307/2529876): the random-effects linear model y = X beta + Z u + e this verb fits with one random intercept (Laird and Ware, Biometrics 38:963, 1982).
- [doi:10.1093/biomet/58.3.545](https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/58.3.545): restricted maximum likelihood, the default estimator (Patterson and Thompson, Biometrika 58:545, 1971).
- [doi:10.2202/1544-6115.1027](https://doi.org/10.2202/1544-6115.1027): the empirical-Bayes moderated t this verb computes, for coefficients and contrasts (Smyth, Stat Appl Genet Mol Biol 3:3, 2004).
- [doi:10.1093/nar/gkv007](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkv007): limma, whose eBayes(legacy = TRUE), and contrasts.fit with topTable(confint), mzLib reproduces to 1e-8 relative (Ritchie et al., Nucleic Acids Res 43:e47, 2015).
- [doi:10.1016/0197-2456(86)90046-2](https://doi.org/10.1016/0197-2456%2886%2990046-2): the moment estimator of the between-study variance (DerSimonian and Laird, Control Clin Trials 7:177, 1986).
- [doi:10.18637/jss.v036.i03](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v036.i03): metafor, whose rma(method = 'DL') mzLib reproduces to 1e-8 relative (Viechtbauer, J Stat Softw 36(3), 2010).
